name: Donghak Peasant Revolution
info: The Donghak Peasant Revolution was a rising in Korea between January 1894 and December 1895, led by followers of the Donghak religion and joined by aggrieved peasants, against corrupt officials, taxation and foreign influence.

facts.where: Korea, above all Jeolla Province, with fighting also in Chungcheong, Gyeongsang, Gyeonggi, Gangwon and Hwanghae.
facts.period: The Gyojo Shinwon petitions (1892–1893); the Gobu revolt (January 1894); the first revolt and the Treaty of Jeonju (spring 1894); rebel rule in the south (summer 1894); the second revolt and the defeat at Ugeumchi (October–November 1894); executions and mopping-up (December 1894–1895).
facts.figures: Jeon Bong-jun, leader of the revolt; Kim Gae-nam and Son Hwa-jung, his generals; Choe Sihyeong, the second leader of Donghak, who opposed the rebellion; Son Byong-hi, general of the Northern Jeob; Yi Bangeon, a Jeolla rebel leader; Kim Gu, the 'Baby Jeobju'.
facts.outcome: The rebel armies were defeated, mainly by Japanese and government forces, and their leaders were captured and executed. Some of their demands later appeared in the Gabo Reform, and many survivors joined the Righteous Armies or the independence movement.

t: The revolution began as a revolt against the abuses of Jo Byeong-gap, the magistrate of Gobu, and grew into a rising across Korea whose leaders were Donghak believers and whose armies were largely peasants.

After the Treaty of Jeonju of May 1894, the rebels ran much of south-west Korea through local offices called Jibgangso, until the arrival of Qing and Japanese troops and then the Japanese victory at Ugeumchi ended their hopes.

The rebel leaders were hanged in March 1895 and thousands of rebels were killed; some of their demands, such as the remarriage of widows and the freeing of enslaved people, were taken up in the Gabo Reform.
dyk: The rebels of 1894 followed rules that included not killing the innocent and paying for food in money rather than taking it, and they wore mostly white and carried bamboo spears, which gave rise to the saying "When sitting, a white mountain; when standing, a bamboo mountain."
ev: Southern Donghak believers petition for the religion's recognition and for the restoration of the honour of its founder
Rebels led by Jeon Bong-jun rise at Gobu against Jo Byeong-gap and defeat government forces at Hwangtojae and the Hwangryong River
The Treaty of Jeonju ends the first revolt, and the rebels govern much of the south-west
Qing and Japanese troops land at Incheon, and the First Sino-Japanese War begins
The rebel army is defeated at the Battle of Ugeumchi, and Jeon disbands it after Taein
At Jonggok on 18 December Japanese forces kill about 2,500 of 2,600 rebels, according to Japanese sources
Jeon Bong-jun and three other leaders are hanged for treason on 29 March

sections.background:
In the late 19th century Korean society faced inequality, corruption and excessive taxation. These problems sparked a series of peasant-led rebellions, which began with the Gwanseo Peasant War and weakened the Joseon government's control of regions outside Hanseong. Secret societies also formed, among them the Salbangye, the 'Association of the Killers of the Yangban (aristocrats)', and the Nokrimdang, 'noble thieves' who stole from the rich and gave to the poor.

In this period the Donghak religion was formed by Choe Je-u, who described a voice that told him to teach its word and gave him a talisman to save people from disease. Donghak was a mixture of religions: its monotheism, sacred books and organised religion resemble Christianity, while its chants and the Sword Dance came from shamanism and folk belief. Choe said that "All humans are Hanulnim", promoted human equality and taught that the world was a cycle of 5,000 years that was ending to make way for a new world. The Joseon dynasty banned the religion and executed him for 'Tricking and Lying to the Foolish People.'

Donghak spread across Gyeongsang Province by the 1870s and was organised into Jeob and Po. In 1871 Yi Pil-je, Jeobju of Yeonghae, revolted using Donghak's organisation; the revolt failed, and Choe Sihyeong, the second leader, then carried the religion to Chungcheong and Jeolla, where Son Hwa-jung, Son Byong-hi, Kim Gae-nam and Jeon Bong-jun were converted.
sections.aims:
By the 1890s Donghak believers were petitioning to overturn the charges on which Choe Je-u had been executed. The religion had split into a Northern Jeob and a Southern Jeob. Seo Inju, leader of the Southern Jeob, asked Choe Sihyeong, the Gyoju, for a petition, but Choe did not answer, presumably remembering the effects of Yi Pil-je's revolt. In November 1892 Jeon Bong-jun led the Samrye Petition, which asked that Donghak not be banned, that Western missionaries and merchants be expelled and that corrupt officials be killed.

At Boeun, about 80,000 believers gathered under flags reading "Expel Westerners and Japanese" and built an earthen fortress. Their requests included restoring the honour of Choe Je-u, ending the persecution of believers, chasing away colonial powers, halting foreign imports, removing the Min family from power, lowering taxes and banning the Dangojeon coin. Northern leaders such as Choe Sihyeong and Son Byong-hi feared executions and stopped the petition within three days.

In 1894 the rebels in arms gave four guidelines, including not killing the innocent, defeating the Japanese and marching on Seoul to kill the Min family. The twelve requests accepted at the Treaty of Jeonju asked for punishment of corrupt officials and of yangban and seonbi, freedom for slaves and for the Cheonmin class, legal remarriage for widows, lower taxes, the picking of politicians by qualities rather than families, the cancelling of debts and land for all peasants.
sections.events:
The immediate cause of the Gobu revolt was the conduct of the local official Jo Byeong-gap. Jeon later listed his misdeeds, among them water taxes for a new reservoir, fines for invented offences and the building of a monument to his father at the peasants' expense. In January 1894 about a thousand rebels occupied the government office, freed prisoners, returned taxed property and destroyed the reservoir, until Jo's replacement persuaded them to disband. In March Jeon and Kim Gae-nam returned with an army that grew to tens of thousands, took Taein and Buan, and defeated government forces at Hwangtojae and the Hwangryong River.

After the rebels took Jeonju Fortress, the government asked for Qing and Japanese help. Qing and Japanese forces landed at Incheon in May, and the dispute over the Convention of Tientsin led to the First Sino-Japanese War. On 7 May the Treaty of Jeonju ended the siege. That summer the rebels ruled most of the south-west through Jibgangso, local offices with a council, scribes and police.

With Japanese troops occupying Seoul, Jeon sought the Northern Jeob's help. Choe Sihyeong had opposed rebellion, but on 12 October the two armies marched on Gongju. After defeat at Ugeumchi on 9 and 10 November and at Taein, Jeon dissolved the army on 28 November. Fighting went on elsewhere into 1895, and the leaders were captured in December and executed in March.
sections.people:
Jeon Bong-jun was Jeobju of Gobu and became the revolt's leader, with Kim Gae-nam and Son Hwa-jung as generals. Along with Choe Gyeong-seon and Kim Deokmyeong they are known as the Five Donghak Generals. In his testimony after capture Jeon emphasised that Donghak believers formed only a small part of the rebels, most of whom were peasants seeking vengeance. Choe Sihyeong, the Gyoju, was staunchly anti-rebel and feared that a large rebellion would end with the destruction of Donghak, though he ordered the Northern Jeob to rise on 12 October. Son Byong-hi led the Northern Jeob as its general.

Other leaders held regions of their own: Yi Bangeon in Jangheung, Kim Inbae in the south coast, Cha Giseok among the guerrillas of Gangwon and Kim Gu in Hwanghae, called the 'Baby Jeobju' because he was 18. Many of the Hwanghae rebels were gold miners; a Japanese lieutenant, Suzuku, sorted them into 'True', 'Temporary' and 'False' Donghak.

Against the rebels stood magistrates such as Jo Byeong-gap, government commanders such as Hong Gyehun, Confucian scholars such as Maeng Yeongjae, who put down Cha Giseok's rising, and Japanese battalions. Yi Yihwa sees the council of a Jibgangso as a rudimentary democracy, while the Joseon scholar Hwang Hyeon, in the Ohagimun, recorded rapes, torture and arson by the rebels out of vengeance against the ruling castes.
sections.outcomes:
The rebels lacked modern weapons. At Ugeumchi they had bows, spears, swords and seventeenth-century-style muskets against Japanese cannon and rifles. Of an army put at 200,000 only 500 remained when the rebels retreated; other figures for the rebels' strength differ and recent estimates give about 50,000. At Taein the Japanese firepower destroyed the rebels and, in the historian Park Eunsik's words, left "nothing left in Taein for 40 kilometers".

Repression was heavy. Japanese sources report that 2,500 of 2,600 rebels died at Jonggok on 18 December 1894; some scholars prefer the term Jonggok Massacre. At the Seokdae Fields 2,000 rebels were killed, and as 800 Japanese soldiers moved through the south-west they killed 600 civilians in a scorched-earth campaign. Cha Giseok was beheaded, Kim Gae-nam was beheaded and his body torn apart, and Jeon Bong-jun and three other leaders were hanged on 29 March 1895. Rebels were also killed in 1895 by being chained together and buried alive in pits or drowned in the sea, and by being torn apart with horses or cows.

The last battle was on Mount Daedun on 17 February 1895, where 30 rebels held out for three days and only a child survived. Choe Sihyeong was captured in April 1898 and executed after a speedy trial.
sections.legacy:
Some rebel demands, including the remarriage of widows and the freeing of enslaved people, were included in the Gabo Reform. The reform was not supported, however, because it did not include land reform, which was the peasants' greatest need. Many rebels later joined the Righteous Army; those of 1905 and 1907 were almost entirely made up of former rebels. Jeon Haesan, the most famous of the Jeolla Righteous Army leaders, was often called the 'son of Jeon Bong-jun'; the North Korean textbook traces a 'patriotic line' from the Jeon family, and the South Korean Ministry of Education calls this revisionism meant to glorify Kim Il Sung. Kim Gu became one of the most respected Korean leaders.

Son Byong-hi became the third patriarch and renamed Donghak 'Cheondoism' to escape persecution as 'rebels'. Cheondoism was legalised in 1905, and Son was imprisoned in 1919 for leading the March 1st Movement and died in prison.

The name of the revolution is disputed. Some hold that it was fundamentally a Donghak revolt, as South Korea's military government did; others, as North Korea officially does, that it was a peasant revolt, citing Jeon's testimony "There were many angered peasants and few Donghak"; the present South Korean position calls it the Donghak Peasant Revolution, since the leaders were Donghak and the armies peasants. Historians also disagree over whether the Great Regent Heungseon secretly backed the rising, which the Russian envoy Hitrovo's message suggested, and over a link to the Japanese Genyosha, which Korean historians largely reject.

summary: The Donghak Peasant Revolution was a rising in Korea in 1894 and 1895, led by followers of the Donghak religion and joined by peasants angered by corruption and taxation. It held much of the south-west until Japanese and government forces defeated it, and its leaders were executed.
references: Stewart Lone, Korea Since 1850 (Longman Cheshire Pty Limited, 1993)
notes: The article gives the rising's dates as 11 January 1894 to 25 December 1895 but says the Gobu rebels gathered on 10 January 1894 and has the last battle on 17 February (1895) and the executions in March 1895; start 1894 and end 1895 are used.
Choe Je-u's execution is dated 1863 in one place and 1864 in another; the year is left out.

Rebel army sizes vary widely in the article (25,000–200,000 at Gongju; 40,000 then 10,000 at Non Stream; 'about 50,000' by recent estimates); the text says figures differ. The article names a Japanese 'Seito' in one passage and 'Saito' in another; omitted.

Kim Gae-nam's conversion is given as 1890 and as 1891 in garbled wording; left out. The article says Kim Gu was 18 but also gives Kim Inbae's date of death and Taein events with some inconsistency in numbers (400 rebels killed, forty houses); only the Park Eunsik quote is used.

Left out as thin or editorialising in the article: the 'cultish' wording and the 2004 Jeollabuk-do compensation law controversy; 'war crimes' are given only as Hwang Hyeon's record; the Buddha's navel legend, folk songs, films and the manhwa lists (popular culture). The statement that the Chinese 'Self-Strengthening Movement' ended is left out.

The 'Seito/Saito' Genyosha material and the claim that the Great Regent backed the rising are mentioned only as disputed. The article says the revolution ended with Christmas 1894 (Yi Bangeon) and gives the 1895 killing methods without a source; stated as the article lists them.
The checker may flag Korean names and place spellings (Jeob, Po, Jibgangso, Hanulnim) as article forms; 'Hanseong' and 'Seoul' are both used as the article has them.
